title: Chapter 7: The Prideful 2
content:
Chapter 7

The Prideful 2

If the sky got any darker, you wouldn’t be able to take two steps through this mountain timber without carrying a torch. Wei Wuxian had been hiking for a while now, yet he hadn’t crossed paths with more than a couple of wandering cultivators. He found it genuinely baffling: were half the clans still down at Buddha’s Foot Town running their mouths and arguing in circles, while the rest turned tail and slunk home empty-handed like that bruised bunch from earlier?

Out of nowhere, desperate shouts for help cut through the tree line ahead.

“Someone! Anyone!”

“Help! Please!”

Men and women were hollering together, their voices thick with raw, frantic panic—hardly the sound of an act. Out in the middle of a desolate mountain wilderness, nine out of ten cries for help were malicious spirits mimicking mortals to lure gullible idiots into a meat grinder.

Naturally, Wei Wuxian was thrilled.

The nastier the evil, the better—his only worry was that it wouldn't be wicked enough!

He kicked the donkey into a trot toward the racket. Looking left and right turned up nothing, but the moment he tilted his head back, there they were. No bloodthirsty specter, no demonic abomination—just that ragged family of rogue cultivators from the well by the fields, bundled together and hauled into the canopy inside an enormous, shimmering golden net.

The middle-aged leader had been trying to guide the younger generation on a scouting sweep through the woods. Instead of catching a whiff of the prey they were praying for, they’d stumbled straight into some rich bastard’s snare and ended up strung from the branches like drying sausage, wailing in misery. Catching sight of an approaching figure, their faces lit up with wild hope—only to plunge into utter despair the second they recognized the local lunatic. The cordage of a Deity-Binding Net was gossamer-thin, but woven from top-shelf materials and virtually unbreakable; once snagged, whether mortal, god, demon, fiend, or phantom, you were stuck thrashing around until someone chopped it open with an even higher-grade spiritual relic. Let alone cutting them down, this painted idiot probably couldn't even tell what he was looking at.

Just as they were about to yell at him to fetch real help, a crisp rustle of parting branches swept through the undergrowth. Darting out from the pitch-black timber came a youth clad in light, elegant robes.

The young master bore a vermilion cinnabar mark right between his brows. His features were aristocratic and handsome, though pinched with a sharp, spiteful edge. He was barely an adolescent, roughly the same age as Lan Sizhui—still practically a kid. A quiver of fletched arrows and a longsword humming with radiant gold light were slung across his back, while his fingers loosely gripped a hunting bow. The embroidery along his tunic was exquisitely lavish, blooming across his chest into a magnificent, sprawling white peony stitched in glittering gold thread that caught the dark night air.

Wei Wuxian inwardly whistled: Stinking rich!

This had to be one of the young masters of the Lanling Jin Sect. Only the Jin clan sported the "Sparks Amidst Snow" white peony as their family crest, likening themselves to the sovereign of all blooms to subtly advertise their self-proclaimed status as the monarchs of the entire cultivation world. And only they dotted their foreheads with red cinnabar, waxing poetic about "illuminating the mind and illuminating the world with vermilion radiance".

The boy had nocked an arrow, ready to draw, but his face fell into deep disgust the moment he saw his net had only snared humans. Disappointment curdled instantly into blistering irritation: “Every single time, it’s you brainless freeloaders! There are over four hundred Deity-Binding Nets strung across this mountain, and before I’ve bagged a single beast, you worthless clowns have already tripped and ruined more than a dozen of them!”

Wei Wuxian was still stuck on the first thought: Seriously, stinking rich!

A single Deity-Binding Net cost a small fortune; throwing down four hundred of them in one go would drive a minor clan straight into bankruptcy. Classic Lanling Jin behavior. But blanket-rigging the entire forest with indiscriminate traps wasn't a hunt—it was a hostile takeover, aggressively boxing everyone else out so nobody could poach a scrap of the prize. It seemed the cultivators scurrying down the slopes earlier hadn’t fled because the phantom was too terrifying, but because the premier clans were simply too obnoxious to cross.

Over the past few days on the road, topped off by the colorful tavern gossip down in Buddha's Foot Town, Wei Wuxian had picked up quite a bit about how the balance of power had shifted. As the supreme victors of the great war that tore the cultivation world apart, the Lanling Jin Sect now called all the shots, with their clan leader reigning supreme under the title of "Chief Cultivator". The Jin clan had always been haughty and obsessed with ostentatious luxury; decades of sitting uncontested on the throne had spoiled their younger generation rotten, breeding a crop of arrogant brats who threw their weight around without consequence. Lesser clans had no choice but to swallow their pride and take the abuse, and backwater family outfits like this couldn't afford to offend them in their wildest dreams. So despite the boy’s foul tongue, the family hanging in the canopy could only flush red, not daring to talk back.

The middle-aged leader swallowed his pride and begged, “Please, young master, have some mercy and let us down.”

Frustrated that his quarry hadn’t shown itself, the boy was more than happy to use these bumpkins as a punching bag. He crossed his arms with a cold sneer. “Hang there and rot. It’ll keep you from bumbling around and ruining my hunt! Once I bag the soul-eating beast, if I remember you’re up there, maybe I’ll come cut you loose.”

If they were truly left swinging in the canopy all night, and whatever nightmare prowling Dafan Mountain happened to stumble across them, they’d be completely defenseless—sitting ducks waiting to have their souls sucked dry. Terrified out of her wits, the round-faced girl who’d gifted Wei Wuxian the apple burst into quiet, trembling tears.

Wei Wuxian had been sitting cross-legged on the donkey’s back. The second that pathetic weeping reached the donkey’s twitching ears, the beast lurched forward and bolted!

Not only did it charge, it let out an ear-splitting bray. If the screech hadn't been so gratingly obnoxious, that reckless, charging momentum wouldn't look out of place on a legendary warhorse. Caught completely off-guard, Wei Wuxian was dumped flat over its tail, hitting the dirt hard enough to nearly crack his skull.

The donkey lowered its skull and charged the Jin boy headfirst, apparently entirely convinced it could ram the brat into orbit. The boy’s arrow was already on the string; he swung his bow round, lining up a shot straight between the beast’s eyes. Unwilling to go hunting for another mount so soon, Wei Wuxian scrambled up and yanked frantically on the tether.

The boy took one look at his face, and his eyebrows shot up in shock. Then, his lips twisted into raw, venomous sneer. “Oh. It’s you.”

Two parts astonishment, eight parts disgust—the sheer venom made Wei Wuxian blink in confusion.

The boy sneered, “What, you got kicked back to your backwater village and finally lost your damn mind? Look at that hideous paint—how dare you show your face in public!”

Hold on a second. Did he just spill some massive tea?!

Don't tell me… Wei Wuxian slapped his thigh in realization. Could Mo Xuanyu’s deadbeat father not be some random minor sect leader, but the infamous Jin Guangshan himself?!

Jin Guangshan had been the previous leader of the Lanling Jin Sect, long since buried. To put it mildly, the man was a piece of work. He had been saddled with a terrifying, politically connected wife, and his henpecked misery was legendary. But terrified as he was, it had never stopped him from sleeping around; even Madam Jin couldn’t keep a leash on him twenty-four hours a day. From aristocratic maidens to rural courtesans, if it moved, he pursued it. Worse, he was as fickle as the wind; the moment he got bored, he tossed his conquests aside without a scrap of responsibility, littering the realm with unacknowledged bastards. Out of that endless sea of illegitimate children, only one had proved brilliant enough to be dragged into the family fold: the current Chief Cultivator and Sect Leader, Jin Guangyao.

Even Jin Guangshan’s demise had been deeply sordid. Deluding himself that he was still in his prime, the old degenerate had tried to push his limits in a chaotic orgy and died of an undignified stroke right in the saddle. It was so thoroughly mortifying that the Lanling Jin Sect had publicly declared the old patriarch died of overwork, while the rest of the cultivation world politely looked the other way, pretending they believed the lie. In short, that was the real reason behind his enduring fame.

Back during the Grand Siege of the Burial Mounds, Jin Guangshan had contributed the most firepower second only to Jiang Cheng. And now, here was Wei Wuxian, piloting the corpse of Jin Guangshan’s own discarded son. Life truly had a sick sense of humor.

Seeing the lunatic staring blankly into space, the boy snapped in disgust, “Get lost already! Looking at you makes me want to puke, you filthy cutsleeve.”

By family lineage, Mo Xuanyu was technically an uncle or an elder to this snot-nosed kid. Getting talked down to by a junior was bad enough; Wei Wuxian decided that even if he didn't care about his own pride, he owed it to this stolen body to push back.

He drawled, “You’ve clearly got a mother who birthed you, but no mother who raised you.”

The insult hit like a spark to dry kindling. Blinding rage flared behind the boy's eyes. He ripped the longsword from his back, his voice deadly and low: “What—did you—say?”

The blade blazed with a brilliant golden aura—a masterwork of spiritual craftsmanship that smaller clans could only dream of laying eyes on, let alone owning. Wei Wuxian squinted at it, an odd tug of familiarity tickling the back of his mind. But he’d seen plenty of high-tier swords with golden spiritual glares in his time, so he didn’t dwell on it. Instead, his fingers twitched around a crude cloth pouch in his palm.

It was a makeshift Spirit-Locking Pouch he’d cobbled together from scrap rags a couple of days ago.

The boy lunged, slashing his blade downward. Wei Wuxian slipped out a paper figure cut in the shape of a man, side-stepped the strike with fluid grace, and slapped the talisman flush against the kid’s spine!

The boy was fast, but Wei Wuxian was an old hand at tripping legs and sticking curses to people’s backs; his sleight of hand was infinitely faster. The kid’s back instantly seized up under an unnatural, crushing weight. His knees buckled, slamming him face-first into the dirt as his prized sword clattered uselessly out of reach. No matter how hard he clawed at the forest floor, he couldn’t lift himself an inch, pinned down as if an entire mountain had dropped onto his spine.

Clinging to his back was a gluttonous spirit that had died of overeating, pressing every ounce of its post-mortem bulk onto the boy’s lungs. Small-time phantoms were weak, but more than enough to handle an arrogant little brat.

Wei Wuxian picked up the fallen golden sword, weighed it in his palm, and with a clean, effortless flick, slashed the hanging net overhead to ribbons.

The captive family tumbled to the ground in a bruised heap. Without a single word, they scrambled to their feet and sprinted down the mountain for dear life. The round-faced girl looked back, wanting to thank him, but her elder yanked her arm so hard her feet barely touched the grass, terrified that sticking around would only draw deeper wrath from the young master.

Pinned in the mud, the boy howled, “You disgusting freak! Just because your spiritual roots are trash and you couldn’t cut it in cultivation, you turned to wicked sorcery! You just wait—do you have any idea who came to this mountain today?! Today, I’m going to—”

Wei Wuxian clutched his chest with dramatic, zero-effort terror. “Oh no! I’m shaking in my boots!”

Back in the day, the heterodox path he pioneered had been heavily vilified for corroding the practitioner’s spiritual foundation over time. Yet because it offered rapid results without being gated by natural talent or spiritual aptitude, it remained irresistibly tempting. People hungry for shortcuts had never stopped dabbling in the dark arts under the table. Naturally, the kid assumed Mo Xuanyu had turned to crooked cultivation out of bitter spite after being kicked out of Lanling. It was a completely logical assumption, and it saved Wei Wuxian a mountain of explaining.

The boy strained against the dirt, his face flushing crimson, and snarled through gritted teeth, “Take this off me right now or I’ll tell my uncle! You’re a dead man!”

Wei Wuxian tilted his head. “Why your uncle and not your dad? And who the hell is your uncle anyway?”

From the dark woods behind him, a voice sliced through the silence—three parts frost, seven parts pure malice:

“I am his uncle. Any last words?”

The sheer sound of that voice sent every drop of blood rushing straight to Wei Wuxian’s head, only to drain away just as fast. Fortunately, his face was already caked in clown-white powder; going pale under that paint was completely invisible.

A young man in deep purple robes strolled out of the timber. His sleeves were bound tight in an archer’s cut, his hand resting casually against the hilt of his sword. A silver bell dangled from his sash, swinging in complete silence as he walked.

He had sharp, almond-shaped eyes framed by thin brows—a dangerous, razor-edged handsomeness. His gaze burned cold and aggressive, sizing up anyone in his path like two bolts of lightning. Stopping ten paces from Wei Wuxian, he stood motionless, wound tight like an arrow drawn to full cheek, carrying himself with an icy, suffocating arrogance.

He scowled down at the dirt. “Jin Ling, what took you so long? Did you really need me to come out here and fetch you? Look at the pathetic state you’re in. Get up off the ground, now!”

Once the initial shock faded, Wei Wuxian recovered his senses. He twitched his fingers inside his wide sleeve, dispelling the paper charm.

Feeling the crushing weight lift, Jin Ling scrambled up, grabbed his sword, and bolted behind Jiang Cheng. He pointed a trembling, furious finger at Wei Wuxian. “I’m breaking your legs!”

Standing side-by-side, the uncle and nephew shared a faint, unmistakable resemblance around the brow and eyes, looking more like brothers than different generations. Jiang Cheng flicked a finger, and the paper man flew right out of Wei Wuxian’s sleeve into his waiting palm. Taking one look at the talisman, Jiang Cheng’s gaze flared with pure venom. He squeezed, and the paper burst into vicious flames, reducing the screeching spirit to ash.

Jiang Cheng’s voice turned deadly soft. “Break his legs? Didn't I teach you? Whenever you cross vermin who dabble in this crooked trash, you slaughter them on the spot and feed the scraps to your dogs!”

Wei Wuxian didn't even bother grabbing the donkey’s reins; he kicked off the dirt and vaulted backward. He had assumed that after so many years, whatever monstrous hatred Jiang Cheng harbored would have faded with time. But life was never that generous. Far from mellowing out, Jiang Cheng’s grudge had aged like venomous wine, curdling into a toxic obsession that lashed out at anyone who even remotely mimicked Wei Wuxian’s cultivation!

Backed by his uncle, Jin Ling struck with twice the savagery, his blade whistling through the air. Wei Wuxian plunged two fingers into his pouch, ready to counter, when a streak of brilliant azure light tore through the dark like a bolt of lightning. It slammed flush against Jin Ling’s sword, instantly shattering the golden glare into glittering dust.

It wasn't a matter of sword quality—the sheer gap in raw cultivation between the two wielders was astronomical.

Wei Wuxian had timed his dodge to the second, but the concussive spiritual flare threw off his footing. He stumbled, took a header into the leaves, and landed flat on his face—right in front of a pair of pristine, snow-white boots.

He froze. Slowly, painfully, he craned his neck.

The first thing to greet his eyes was a long, crystalline blade that looked carved from pure, unyielding frost.

Across the cultivation sects, that sword was legendary. Wei Wuxian had witnessed its terrifying power countless times—both fighting shoulder-to-shoulder with it and staring down its edge in blood-soaked duels. The hilt was forged from pure, enchanted silver; the blade was impossibly slender and clear as ice, radiating a bone-deep frost that sliced through iron like paper. It looked ethereal and weightless, but in truth, it carried a crushing spiritual mass; ordinary cultivators couldn't even lift it, let alone swing it.

Bichen.

The blade inverted, snapping into its scabbard with a sharp, resonant ring above his head.

At the same time, Jiang Cheng’s icy voice drifted across the clearing: “I wondered who it was. The Second Young Master Lan himself.”

The white boots stepped lightly around Wei Wuxian, measured and unhurried, advancing three paces. Wei Wuxian pushed himself up. As they brushed past each other, his gaze collided with the other man’s for a fleeting, breathless fraction of a second.

The man stood bathed in cascading moonlight, carrying a seven-stringed zither across his back. The instrument was slightly narrower than an ordinary guqin, carved from smooth, jet-black wood.

Bound across his forehead was the Lan ribbon, stitched with rolling cloud patterns. His skin was porcelain-fair, his features so exquisitely refined they seemed sculpted from jade. His eyes were an extraordinarily pale amber, clear as tinted glass, lending his stare a remote, untouchable chill. His expression was pure frost—a rigid, unwavering austerity that didn't so much as flicker at the sight of Wei Wuxian’s ridiculous clown paint.

From head to toe, he was immaculate, untainted by a speck of dust, devoid of the slightest breach of decorum.

Yet the only four words screaming inside Wei Wuxian’s head were:

Walking funeral robes!

Absolute, literal mourning clothes. The cultivation world could praise the Gusu Lan robes to the high heavens, crowning them the most elegant uniform in existence, and they could fawn over Lan Wangji as an untouchable, once-in-a-century beauty—none of it changed the fact that the man walked around with a grim, deadpan expression like his wife had just passed away.

Rotten luck, narrow paths, and old grudges. Misfortunes really never traveled alone.

Lan Wangji didn't say a word, his gaze fixed dead ahead as he stood across from Jiang Cheng. Jiang Cheng was a remarkably striking man in his own right, but standing opposite this figure, he seemed to lose a fraction of his luster, edged out by an air of restless hostility.

Jiang Cheng arched a brow. “Hanguang-jun truly lives up to the reputation of ‘going wherever chaos arises’. What brings you all the way out to these desolate woods tonight?”

Sect leaders and high-ranking cultivators generally turned their noses up at low-level hauntings, but Lan Wangji had always been the lone exception. He never picked or chose his night-hunts based on prestige, nor did he scoff at an entity because slaying it wouldn't boost his fame. If people called for help, he showed up—and he had operated that way since his youth. “To go wherever chaos arises” was the world’s enduring tribute to his character.

Coming out of Jiang Cheng’s mouth, however, the phrase dripped with sarcastic venom.

The Lan disciples who had caught up behind their elder bristled at the disrespect. Lan Jingyi, never one to filter his thoughts, blurted out, “Aren’t you here too, Sect Leader Jiang?”

Jiang Cheng’s eyes iced over. “Tch. Since when do juniors butt in when their elders are speaking? The Gusu Lan Sect prides itself on immaculate etiquette, yet this is how you train your disciples?”

Lan Wangji showed zero interest in entertaining the spat. He cast a quiet glance at Lan Sizhui, who took the cue immediately: let the juniors deal with the juniors.

Sizhui stepped forward, addressing the boy politely: “Young Master Jin, night-hunts have always been a matter of fair competition among the sects. Yet you’ve blanketed Dafan Mountain in snares, leaving other cultivators unable to move without fearing a trap. Does this not violate the rules of the hunt?”

Jin Ling’s arrogant scowl was an exact carbon copy of his uncle’s. “If they’re stupid enough to step into my traps, that’s their problem. We can talk about it after I bag my kill!”

Lan Wangji’s brow furrowed faintly.

Jin Ling opened his mouth to snap again, only to find his jaws locked together—not a single sound could escape his throat. Panic washed over the boy's face. Jiang Cheng looked over, realizing Jin Ling’s lips were sealed tight as if glued shut. Any pretense of manners vanished into pure fury: “Lan! What is the meaning of this?! Jin Ling isn't yours to discipline—undo it now!”

The Silence Spell was the Lan Sect’s signature disciplinary trick for unruly juniors. Wei Wuxian had suffered under this petty hex more times than he could count; while it wasn't particularly advanced, outsiders had no way to crack it. If you tried to force your mouth open, you’d either rip your lips bloody or end up mute for days; your only choice was to sit in quiet reflection until the timer expired.

Lan Sizhui stepped in gently, “Sect Leader Jiang, please don’t be angry. As long as he doesn't try to force it, the seal will lift automatically in the time it takes an incense stick to burn.”

Before Jiang Cheng could bark back, a cultivator clad in Jiang purple burst out of the trees, shouting, “Sect Leader!” Catching sight of Lan Wangji standing in the clearing, the man choked on his words, hesitating.

Jiang Cheng sneered, “Speak. What other wonderful news do you have for me?”

The guest disciple kept his voice low and miserable. “Just moments ago… an azure spiritual blade flew through the forest, dismantling all of our Deity-Binding Nets.”

Jiang Cheng shot a murderous glare at Lan Wangji, the fury written plain across his face. “How many did it break?”

The disciple swallowed hard. “…All of them.”

Over four hundred nets!

Jiang Cheng’s temper boiled over.

This entire expedition had turned into an absolute disaster. He had come out personally tonight just to run interference for Jin Ling. The boy was sixteen this year—the age where juniors made their public debut to build a reputation against their peers. Jiang Cheng had handpicked Dafan Mountain as his personal training ground, stringing traps and intimidating the local competition so Jin Ling could claim the glory uncontested. Four hundred Deity-Binding Nets were monstrously expensive, but pocket change to the Yunmeng Jiang Sect.

Losing the nets was nothing; losing face was unforgivable.

Watching Lan Wangji dismantle his setup without blinking made the bile rise in Jiang Cheng’s throat. His eyes narrowed into slits, his left thumb idly, deliberately brushing across the silver ring worn on his right index finger.

It was a fatal tell.

Everyone in the cultivation world knew that ring was a terrifying, lethal spiritual treasure. The moment the Sect Leader of Jiang started stroking it, murder was on the table.
